pinboard.title: Passkeys are a trap. Do not use them. - by The Hack
Pattern Matching Beats Narrative Reasoning
pinboard.description:
Manual Pattern Matching for Teams

That’s a lot of words to say: “trust your gut!”. But what if you haven’t developed intuition? Or what if your intuition disagrees with the intuition of your team?

There is a slightly more legible approach that I’ve found effective:

Look at your past bets and ask yourself: what are the 10-20 attributes that mattered? List them out, and then go through each of your winning and losing bets, noticing which attributes they had.

We did this for all the product feature bets we made at Spellbook, and were able to correlate 16 attributes with what made a successful product bet. And many were surprising.




Almost none of our correlated attributes had to do with the narrative of the feature itself. We discovered a bunch of other things that mattered:

Can a lawyer get value from the feature instantly with absolutely zero configuration?
Was someone on the team so inspired to build something that they “started without permission”?
Is the feature “whole” rather than a stepping stone to get somewhere else?
Can the feature be fully prototyped in 2 weeks?
We ended up with a framework that is a middle ground between legible, narrative based reasoning and intuition. And the best part is we could objectively score prospective bets in this framework.

It brings us a little closer to reasoning like a chess engine. These signals increased our hit rate significantly when we used to not hit at all.

For years we had been listening to the gospel: “talk to your customers! Build what they ask for!” This was helpful, but it had an catastrophic blindspot that was causing us to make losing bets for years.

We were missing an entire universe of patterns outside of the tunnel vision of stories.

pinboard.title: @lugaricano: The biggest, and stupidest, myth in European politics, particularly popular in France, is that Europe suffers the consequences of "austerity" and "neoliberalism". In the biggest 5 countries in Europe, more than half of the population makes it
pinboard.description:
@lugaricano
The biggest, and stupidest, myth in European politics, particularly popular in France, is that Europe suffers the consequences of "austerity" and "neoliberalism". In the biggest 5 countries in Europe, more than half of the population makes its income from the state, less than half from the private sector. This is what makes the problem of reducing the welfare state so impossible: more than half of the voters are net recipients. No surprise that Italy's budget has not been balanced in 100 years, France's in 50 years (ooh la la, l'austérité!!):
-France: 30 million from the state versus 21m private sector workers. State spending is 57% of GDP, taxes more than half the economy. The budget hasn't been balanced in the lifetime of most French (since 1974).
- Germany: 35 million adults from the state, versus 34 million from the private sector. 10% of the population is registered as severely disabled. Public spending is over half of GDP. Germany has had a continuous budget deficit since 2019.
-Italy: 23 million from the state, versus  20.5 million private-sector workers. Public spending is 51% of GDP.  Italy has had a budget deficit every year since 1925, for 100 years.
- Spain more people get their income from the state since 2024: 18.21 million from the public sector versus 17.9 million people working in the private sector. Since 2025, Spain also had more government employees than self-employed workers (autónomos) for the first time in history. State spending is at 45%, budget has not been balanced since 2007.
- UK: 54% of households now receive more in state benefits than they pay in taxes. State spending is 44.5% of GDP, taxes (40%) are at their highest since 1950, the budget hasn't been balanced since 2001, and 1 in 5 new cars is paid by the government through a bizarre state disability scheme (Motability).

pinboard.title: The more we rely on tech, the more we deskill our bodies | Aeon Essays
pinboard.description:
I have come to believe that our bodily deskilling is, in many ways, a loss of faith in what it is to be alive. A life of physical effort and friction is not only unavoidable if we want to be as resilient and capable as possible, but it is, in a nontrivial sense, the source of our intelligence.
We have fallen into habits that are steadily deskilling the human body, eroding capacities honed by evolution to support our wellbeing as we move through the world. Some of these capacities are weakening through disuse: we have come to rely on our phones, for example, and now, increasingly, on AI, to rapidly do work that would once have required something more physical – like looking around, or asking someone, or going to find and consult a book. Reliance on GPS may weaken both our spatial attention and the fluency of our wayfinding. In surrendering to a quick technological fix, we are, moment by moment, doing less sensing, navigating, remembering, walking, choosing, and attending. Other capacities are being retrained by machines and algorithms to work against us: for instance, smartphones and chatbots can train us to keep reaching for them even when we no longer enjoy using them, turning a conscious choice into an automatic habit and a colossal waste of time. The body that results is less able to assess its own condition, improvise and regulate itself. The crucial distinction is between technologies that strengthen our capacities and those that repeatedly substitute for the actions through which those capacities are formed.

Charlie Munger shares opinion of Tesla CEO Elon Musk
pinboard.description:
from Daring Fireball

Re: my post today on the still-vaporware Tesla Roadster and Benedict Evans’s maxim that “Elon Musk is a bullshitter who delivers”, a reader sent me this YouTube short of Charlie Munger’s answer to a question at Berkshire Hathaway’s 2020 shareholder meeting regarding Tesla’s volatility and Musk’s self-promotion. Munger said:

My thoughts are two. I would never buy it, and I would never sell it short.

[Audience laughs.]

I have a third comment. There was a man out in Los Angeles for years named Howard Ahmanson. He once said something that I’ve taken to my heart: “Never underestimate the man who overestimates himself.” I think Elon Musk is peculiar and he may overestimate himself, but he may not be wrong all the time.

 ★

Author Susanna Clarke: in defence of fantasy fiction
pinboard.description: "There is a danger associated with growing up, of putting aside children’s books. We must be careful lest all we are left with is a world that is very much not alive, a natural world that is mere piles of stuff – stuff that people can use or not use, preserve or destroy, just as they want. When Lewis wrote about giants rising from the mountains of Mourne, it was a Romantic idea. There was nothing very practical about it. We weren’t yet aware of climate change; the natural world was not yet in crisis; species were not going extinct at the rate they are today. Now we need an idea of the natural world as something that has value and life of its own, quite independent of us. This would have been so obvious to people in the past that it would not have been worth stating, but 200 years after the Industrial Revolution our sight has become a little clouded."
